english: Six distinct beads, of which three are red and three are blue, are strung together to form a necklace, all distinct necklaces being equally likely. Let $p$ be the probability that red and blue beads alternate on the necklace, and let $q$ be the probability that the three red beads are consecutive on the necklace. Then the value of $p-q$ is ______.
hindi: छः भिन्न मनकों को, जिनमें तीन लाल तथा तीन नीले हैं, एक साथ पिरोकर एक हार बनाया जाता है, सभी भिन्न हार समसम्भाव्य हैं। माना कि $p$ हार पर लाल तथा नीले मनकों के एकान्तर क्रम में होने की प्रायिकता है, तथा $q$ तीनों लाल मनकों के हार पर क्रमागत होने की प्रायिकता है। तब $p-q$ का मान ______ है।
solution: Necklaces of 6 distinct beads: $\dfrac{(6-1)!}{2}=60$ (rotations and turning over identified)
Alternate: round-table count $2!\cdot3!=12$ (fix one red; other reds in the alternate places), necklaces $\dfrac{12}{2}=6$
Reds consecutive: block of reds ($3!$) with 3 blues: $3!\cdot3!=36$ round-table arrangements, necklaces $18$
solution_full: A necklace can be rotated and turned over. For $n$ distinct beads, there are $(n-1)!$ circular arrangements up to rotation, and turning over pairs them (no arrangement of distinct beads with $n\geq3$ is its own mirror image), so there are $\dfrac{(n-1)!}{2}$ necklaces. For $n=6$: $\dfrac{120}{2}=60$.

Both properties (alternating colours, reds consecutive) are unchanged by rotation and by turning over, so in each case the number of necklaces is half the number of circular arrangements up to rotation.

Alternating: fix one red bead to remove rotations; the other two reds must be at the positions 2 and 4 places away (2! orders), and the blues fill the remaining 3 positions ($3!$). That gives $12$ arrangements and $6$ necklaces.
Reds consecutive: treat the reds as a block ($3!$ inner orders); with the 3 blues there are 4 units around a circle, $(4-1)!=6$ arrangements. That gives $36$ arrangements and $18$ necklaces.
originality_note: New: two restricted necklace counts (alternating colours, one colour in a block) compared through probabilities over the 60 necklaces, which needs the 'reflection preserves the property' argument for each count (way 5). Closest known: 'n boys and n girls alternately round a table' and AMC-type bead arrangement probabilities. Different because: the objects are necklaces, so the denominator and both numerators must each be halved for the right reason.
blueprint_concepts: Circular permutations; clockwise/anticlockwise; necklace and garland

concept_use.Circular permutations; clockwise/anticlo: The sample space and both events are counted as necklaces (rotation and turning over identified), (n-1)!/2.
concept_use.Circular arrangements with restrictions: The two restrictions are the 'alternating' and 'together' circular arrangements with distinct beads.
